## Beyond the switch

- In chapters 4 and 5, the treatment is **binary and absorbing**: once a unit is treated,
  it remains treated.
- Two other cases are frequent:
  - a **dose**: the treatment has an intensity;
  - **on and off**: the treatment starts, stops, and may start again.
- Dose: **the China shock** (Autor et al. 2013). US local labour markets are exposed to
  Chinese imports according to their industry mix.
- On and off: **newspapers and democracy** (Gentzkow et al. 2011). According to models of
  voting under imperfect information, better-informed citizens vote more. Gentzkow et al.
  test this prediction on US counties that gain and lose daily newspapers between 1869 and
  1928 (before radio and television, the newspaper was the main source of political
  information), and find that turnout rises with the number of newspapers.

\vfill
\footnotesize\emph{References for the whole chapter: Baker, Callaway, Cunningham,
Goodman-Bacon \& Sant'Anna (2026), Appendix A; Callaway, Goodman-Bacon \& Sant'Anna
(2024); de Chaisemartin \& D'Haultfœuille (2020, 2024).}

# Doses

## TWFE with a dose

$$ y_{it}=f_i+f_t+\beta\,D_i\cdot\text{Post}_t+u_{it} $$

- The usual regression puts the dose in place of the treatment dummy: **one coefficient**
  for all doses.
- First problem: **some doses count more than their number of units.** $\hat\beta$
  averages the effects of all doses with weights that differ from the share of units at
  each dose (Callaway et al. 2024).
- Second problem: $\hat\beta$ compares units with different doses. Such a comparison
  mixes two effects of a dose, which require different assumptions.

## Two effects of a dose

- $\text{ATT}(d\mid d)$: the effect of the dose $d$ on the units that received it.
- $\text{ACRT}(d\mid d)$: the effect of **one more unit** of dose on those units, the slope
  of the dose-response.
- China shock: the job loss of a highly exposed market, against the extra loss from a
  little more exposure.

## Two effects, two assumptions

\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{2.6cm} >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{3.1cm} >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{4.9cm}@{}}
\toprule
Effect & Comparison & Assumption\\
\midrule
\textbf{Level} $\text{ATT}(d\mid d)$ & dose $d$ against untreated units & parallel trends: without treatment, units at dose $d$ would have evolved like the untreated\\[6pt]
\textbf{Slope} $\text{ACRT}(d\mid d)$ & dose $d$ against nearby doses & \textbf{strong} parallel trends: all units would respond alike to the same dose\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\vspace{4pt}

- The researcher chooses the assumptions depending on the effect they want to analyse.
- In practice, the level is estimated dose bin by dose bin: a $2\times2$ of each bin
  against the untreated units (Callaway et al. 2024).
- China shock: every market is exposed to Chinese imports, so there is no untreated group.
  Only the second row is available: comparisons between doses, under strong parallel
  trends.

## Without strong parallel trends

\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.85\textwidth]{fig/dose_response.png}
\end{center}

\small

- Solid curve: the $\text{ATT}(d\mid d)$, each point a **different group** of units.
- Its slope adds the causal response and **selection**: the high-dose units respond more.
- Under strong parallel trends, the two curves coincide.

# On and off

## Treatment paths

- When the treatment turns on and off, each unit follows a **path**: treated in some
  periods, untreated in others.
- Each path is a group: with many periods, there are too many groups to compare one by
  one.
- Newspapers: a county can gain a newspaper, lose it, and gain another one later.

## Carryover

\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.72\textwidth]{fig/on_off.png}
\end{center}

\small

- **Carryover**: past treatment still affects the outcome after it stops (blue line).
- Newspapers: a county that loses its newspaper may keep a higher turnout for some
  elections.

## The switchers event study

- de Chaisemartin and D'Haultfœuille (2024) compare the **switchers**, units whose treatment
  changes for the first time, with the **not-yet-switchers**, units whose treatment has not
  changed yet.
- Assumption: without the change, the switchers would have evolved like the
  not-yet-switchers (parallel trends), and they do not react before the change (no
  anticipation).
- The effect $\ell$ periods after the **first change** of treatment: following the actual
  path, against keeping the initial treatment.
- No restriction on carryover: what happens after the first change is part of the effect.
- Newspapers: the effect on turnout $\ell$ elections after a county first gains or loses a
  newspaper.

## Reading the switchers event study

- As in the event study of chapter 4, the estimator gives one coefficient per period
  around the first change:
  - **effects** ($\ell=1,2,\dots$): after the first change;
  - **placebos** ($\ell=-1,-2,\dots$): the same comparison **before** the first change,
    close to zero if parallel trends hold. This is the pre-trend test of chapter 4.
- The effect at $\ell$ includes everything that happened since the first change,
  switch-offs included. Newspapers: a county that gains a newspaper and loses it two
  elections later.
- **Normalized** effects divide by the extra treatment received since the first change:
  the effect of one newspaper, per election.

# Conclusion

## Conclusion

- With a dose, first decide which effect you want: the effect of the dose received needs
  parallel trends, the effect of one more unit of dose needs strong parallel trends.
- When the treatment turns on and off, compare the units whose treatment changes with the
  units whose treatment has not changed yet. Each effect is the effect of the whole path
  since the change.
- In both cases, the TWFE coefficient mixes effects with weights set by the regression: do
  not report it alone.

# In R

## In R: effects and placebos (DIDmultiplegtDYN)

Four lines estimate the effects and the placebos of the switchers event study.

```r
library(data.table); library(fixest); library(DIDmultiplegtDYN)
d <- fread("rica_grippe_td6.csv")[canards_val > 0]             # 1
d[, y := log(canards_val)]                                     # 2
es <- did_multiplegt_dyn(as.data.frame(d), outcome = "y",
        group = "id", time = "annee", treatment = "restriction",
        effects = 8, placebo = 3, cluster = "id")              # 3
es$results$p_jointplacebo                                      # 4
```

\small

- **1**: one row per farm and year; only the years with a positive duck output are kept,
  so that its log exists.
- **2**: the outcome, the log of duck output.
- **3**: switchers against not-yet-switchers: 8 effects after the first change and 3
  placebos before, with standard errors clustered by farm. `es$results$Effects` and
  `es$results$Placebos` give the event-study curve.
- **4**: the joint test that the three placebos are zero.

## In R: normalized effects and TWFE

Two lines estimate the normalized effects and the TWFE coefficient to compare.

```r
nor <- did_multiplegt_dyn(as.data.frame(d), outcome = "y",
        group = "id", time = "annee", treatment = "restriction",
        effects = 8, placebo = 3, cluster = "id",
        normalized = TRUE)                                     # 5
feols(y ~ restriction | id + annee, d, cluster = ~id)          # 6
```

\small

- **5**: the same estimation with `normalized = TRUE`, in which each effect is divided by
  the years of treatment accumulated since the first change.
- **6**: the TWFE coefficient, where the years after the switch-off count as untreated.
